findings.title: Regenerating recovery codes stores the new set in user storage but leaves the previously stored DB codes valid
findings.description:
When `updateCredential` succeeds, `createRecoveryCodesCredential` only logs (lines 126-127). It never removes the recovery credential already stored in Keycloak's DB. Before this change, the regenerate path called `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential`, which deletes the existing stored credential first (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.java:39-40).

Validation still consults the DB store for federated users. `UserCredentialManager.isValid(List)` runs every local `CredentialInputValidator` after the federated one (UserCredentialManager.java:76-77). `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid` accepts any unused code in the stored credential (lines 99-112).

Path: a federated user already has DB-stored codes, for example from a time when user storage did not accept recovery codes. The user regenerates and the user storage accepts. The new set goes upstream, and the old DB set stays. Entering an old code fails the federated validator, then passes the local one, so codes the user believes were revoked still log in.

findings.title: Federated recovery codes are never consumed, so a used code authenticates again
findings.description:
The user-storage validator checks membership with `anyMatch` and returns without marking the code used. Elsewhere recovery codes are single-use: the local path removes the consumed code and writes the credential back (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.java:105-111). Here, `getCredentials` (lines 237-242) rebuilds the credential from the full code list on every read, so `allCodesUsed()` is never true for it. The authenticator's exhaustion branch (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.java:85-92) therefore never runs, and the displayed code number stays at #1 (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.java:17-21).

The defect is in the testsuite fixture, which is the only in-tree federated implementation. The production path (CredentialHelper and the authenticator) also gives federated codes no route to consumption, so the single-use contract is unmet as wired.

findings.title: Raw recovery codes go to user storage in cleartext, while the local path stores only hashes
findings.description:
`createRecoveryCodesCredential` serializes the raw `generatedCodes` list into the user-storage credential. The local path stores only `hashRawCode()` digests (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.java:65-67). The fixture persists that JSON verbatim (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:197) and compares it in plaintext (line 340), so the codes sit unhashed in the external store, while Keycloak's own store never holds them.

Passing raw input is how the SPI works for passwords; the fixture hashes the password itself (lines 147-155). So the fix may belong in the provider. Either way, the helper hands over raw codes without a note, and the two storage paths now keep different secret material.

findings.title: Federated recovery credential is returned with a null id, so admin listing shows `id: null` and deletion cannot match it
findings.description:
`getCredentials` builds the recovery credential with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` (lines 237-241), which never sets an id. `updateCredential` assigns one (line 195), and the OTP branch received the same treatment in this change (line 179), so the id is lost on read.

Downstream, the admin credentials endpoint copies `cred.getId()` (UserResource.java:814-815, ModelToRepresentation.java:665), so the response has `id: null`. `CredentialDeleteHelper.removeCredential` matches federated credentials with `credentialId.equals(c.getId())` (CredentialDeleteHelper.java:64). A delete for this credential can never match and ends in `NotFoundException` (line 81).
